title: MA8-02702
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons for decision in the claim for refugee protection filed by XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXX (the claimant), a citizen of Mexico, who is claiming refugee status under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
In her personal information form (PIF), the claimant alleged the following, specifically in her response to question 31.

The claimant alleged that, in XXXXX 2006, a secret admirer began making harassing telephone calls to her at her home and at her workplace. He even sent her gifts and messages. The claimant alleged that this caused her a great deal of harm. She therefore went to the police to file a complaint against her secret admirer. The claimant alleged that the police officers did not take her complaint seriously and, contemptuously, even said that such things only happen to stars and that she should look at herself in the mirror. The claimant alleged that things calmed down for some time and that she accepted an invitation for a date from XXXX XXXX, a co-worker.

The claimant alleged that, on the morning after her date with Mr. XXXX, her secret admirer called her to tell her that any man who took an interest in her would end up like XXXX XXXX. The claimant alleged that XXXX XXXX had been hospitalized and had been beaten by a man after their date. The claimant alleged that the description that Mr. XXXX gave her was of her maternal uncle, XXXX XXXX XXXX,1 the assailant. She alleged that she wanted XXXX XXXX to file a complaint against her uncle, but he refused to do so, telling her that nothing would come of it because the police would not do anything without a witness. In addition, the police do not open an investigation easily, unless they are given a great deal of money.

The claimant alleged that she continued to receive harassing telephone calls and that she was convinced that it was her uncle. She alleged that she did not want to tell anyone about her situation because she was ashamed. However, the claimant alleged that she decided to talk about her situation with her mother without giving all the details. The claimant alleged that her mother did not believe her and that she was disgusted by the idea that she could think of such a thing.
Fearing for her safety in Mexico, the claimant left her country on XXXXX, 2008, to travel to Canada, where she filed a claim for refugee protection at the port of entry upon arriving. Identity

The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity. She submitted a copy of her passport, which was issued on XXXXX, 2008. This document was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC), and a copy was filed in the record.2 The issue of whether the claimant took the necessary steps in the situation to inform the Mexican authorities is the determinative issue in this case.

The panel took into account Guideline 4 of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) regarding Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.3 The claimant's testimony was extremely emotional. She cried throughout almost the entire hearing. Visibly, and based on her testimony, she was talking about a very sensitive topic, which she had not, as she stated, shared with anyone prior to the hearing, which explains why she amended her PIF to add her uncle's identity shortly before the hearing.

When asked whom she feared in Mexico and asked to further elaborate about her agent of persecution, she answered that she feared XXXX XXXX XXXX, her mother's brother, who lives in the same city as her parents in XXXXX, Mexico. He is a XXXXX XXXXX for the multinational XXXXX. The claimant fears that XXXX XXXX XXXX will continue harassing her should she return to Mexico.

When asked when her problems started, the claimant answered that XXXX XXXX XXXX had touched her when she was only nine years old and that this continued until she was twelve.4 When asked whether the touching continued after the age of twelve, the claimant seemed to state no. However, he allegedly continued to remind her of the touching and, on several occasions, he allegedly stated that she liked to be touched and that, according to XXXX XXXX XXXX, she was a slut.

The claimant also described XXXX XXXX XXXX as someone who was very involved in the community and in the church, who was physically imposing and who had a distinctive voice. When asked why she did not recognize XXXX XXXX XXXX voice during the eight calls that she described-particularly when she described his voice as distinctive-the claimant answered that she did not know why and that perhaps he had disguised his voice. When asked why she never talked to her parents or her two brothers about the touching that she was subjected to, the claimant answered that it was because she was ashamed and that she was sure that her parents, who are very conservative, would not believe her. To give an example of the extent of her parents' conservatism, the claimant testified that when she told her parents that she had become pregnant in Canada with her daughter, XXXX XXXX, who was born on XXXX, 2009, her mother told her that it was a child of the devil, because she was born out of wedlock.

Despite some concerns regarding the late addition of her uncle to her narrative and the fact that she had apparently never told her parents the extent of the serious problems she went through because of him, the panel gives the claimant the benefit of the doubt with respect to the fact that she suffered serious physical and obvious emotional trauma at the hands of XXXX XXXX XXXX. When asked whether she went to see the authorities about the problems she had gone through with her uncle, the claimant answered that she went to the police once, but at that time, she did not know that it was her uncle, thinking it was a secret admirer who was harassing her. The claimant answered that the police officers did not take her seriously, that they told her that these things only happen to celebrities and that they made contemptuous remarks, specifically, that she should look at herself in the mirror.

When asked whether, when she was in Mexico, she went to see any authority at all to directly report XXXX XXXX XXXX by identifying him and by giving the whole story about what she had been through, as she described it during the hearing, the claimant answered that she had not. When asked why she answered the way she did, she stated that it was because she was afraid that he could find out and that he could cause her further harm.

The test for whether state protection might reasonably be forthcoming is an objective one.5 There is a presumption that every state is able to protect its citizens.6 In this case, it was the claimant's responsibility to establish clear and convincing evidence of the absence of state protection. According to the documentary evidence, Mexico is a democracy that functions relatively effectively and that has an independent judicial system. For instance, the documentary evidence indicates that the Mexican authorities generally promote human rights and that they investigate, prosecute, and sentence convicted criminals.7 The panel also took into account that there are other agencies, such as the Comision Nacional de Derechos Humanos (CNDH) that can also carry out studies and investigations and issue recommendations in cases of human rights abuses.8 Clearly, the Mexican system is not perfect, as stated by counsel for the claimant, and this can be particularly difficult for women.9 However, despite the progress Mexico has made in this area,10 the mere fact that these efforts are not always successful is not enough to rebut the presumption of state protection.11 The protection offered by the state must not only be theoretical; it must be adequate and satisfactory.12 In this case, the claimant had an obligation to seek out the protection of the Mexican authorities, unless it was objectively reasonable not to do so; in other words, unless state protection would not have been forthcoming in any case.13

The panel also took into account the fact that the claimant failed to establish that her agent of persecution had an influence on the police and on the workings of the judicial protection system. Unfortunately, the panel will never be able to know whether the claimant presented the whole story of what she experienced at the hands of her agent of persecution to the police, including all the horrible details about the actions and the touching that she experienced from the time she was nine years old or the fact that this individual, twenty or so years later, resumed his abuse against the claimant by making anonymous calls to her and by beating a young man with whom she had gone out for an evening. Unfortunately, the panel will never know whether the claimant could have obtained adequate state protection.

Since the claimant did not report her agent of persecution as part of the full account of the harm she suffered at his hands, she failed to rebut with clear and convincing evidence the availability of state protection for all the problems she had in Mexico.

Despite the finding that the claimant failed to rebut with clear and convincing evidence the presumption of state protection, the panel wants to stress that it was very courageous of the claimant to finally be able to talk about the problems she experienced during her childhood. The panel hopes that she will obtain the necessary assistance to face the problems she had. Unfortunately, the panel could not take these aspects or the fact that the claimant has had a little girl since she has been in Canada into consideration in rendering its decision. Nonetheless, these important aspects could surely be taken into consideration in another forum that has the jurisdiction to consider these aspects.

The panel determines that the claimant, XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXX, is neither a "Convention refugee" under section 96 nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA. For these reasons, her claim for refugee protection is rejected.
